newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian capex seen staying strong.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian capex seen staying strong.

text.p: Investment spending is one of the pillars of Australian economic growth, and economists expect Thursday's December quarter capital expenditure (capex) report from the Australian Bureau of Statistics to throw up further evidence of the economy's 1997 recovery.
Official forecasters remain bullish on investment, with the government last month lifting its forecast for 1996/97 to June 30 to 17 percent growth from an already robust 14 percent.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), which last year called capex "the linchpin of forecast growth," also remains upbeat.

"Recent information supports, and if anything strengthens, the earlier picture that a very solid upswing in investment spending is underway," the RBA said in its quarterly report on the economy released last week.

The median forecast of the 25 economists Reuters surveyed was for a 2.1 percent rise in December quarter capex, following on from the 0.9 percent rise in the September quarter. Forecasts range from a fall of two percent to a rise of 5.0 percent.
Capex is broken into two compoments -- building and structures, and equipment, plant and machinery -- of which the former is expected to have been the strongest in the quarter.
Weakness in capital imports in the December quarter, when they fell over eight percent, is expected to have limited growth in equipment, plant and machinery.
However this is expected to be offset by some signs of an upswing in non-residential construction in the quarter.

"Investment has really been very strong, up 25 percent in the last 12 months, so if we do see another hefty increase in December, we really are looking at a very good investment performance," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said. "That I think is now starting to bear fruit in some of the productivity growth we've been seeing in the economy as well."
But of perhaps more importance than the quarterly data, the capex report will provide an update on the investment outlook.

Capex surveys are conducted in the eight or nine week period after the end of the quarter to which the survey relates, meaning the December quarter survey returns were completed during January and February.
The survey gets three figures from businesses - actual expenditure during the period the survey covers, and a short and long term forecast of expected expenditure.

In the December quarter survey, the short term estimate will be for expected expenditure in 1996/97, the fifth such estimate for expenditure in the year, while the longer term estimate will be the first forecast for expenditure in the 1997/98 year.

Economists will be looking for the 1996/97 estimate to be higher than A$42.910 billion estimate made in the September quarter survey, and for the first estimate of the 1997/98 year to be higher than the A$31.404 billion first estimate for the 1996/97 year, made in the December quarter 1996 survey.
If this pattern emerges, it is seen as supportive of expected growth in investment intentions, which in turn is seen as pointing to economic growth.

While the total level of investment has been strong, it has not been evenly spread over different areas of the economy, explaining some of the patchiness in the economy, analysts said. Over the past year, a lot of it has been concentrated in the capital intensive industries of mining and telecommunications, due to the cable television roll out.

"So while business investment has been strong, it has been quite disparite across sectors, and it's also been very much related to the non-dwelling construction area and mining and infrastructure related projects," National Australia Bank senior economist Jeff Oughton said.
